<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:main}
	For every prime $p\geq3$,
	\[
	H_{p,1/3}\equiv a_p(f_{12.4.a.a})\pmod{p^3},
	\]
	and
	\[
	H_{p,1/6}\equiv a_p(f_{24.4.a.a})\pmod{p^3}.
	\]
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:116-initial}
	For $0\leq k\leq N$, one has
	\[
	v_p(b_{1/6,k})\geq0.
	\]
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
For $k<p$, the factor $(k!)^4$ is a $p$-adic unit.  Each rational
	Pochhammer symbol displayed above contains at most one factor divisible
	by $p$, since the corresponding linear congruence has a unique solution
	modulo $p$.  After clearing the denominators $2$, $3$, and $6$, every
	relevant positive linear factor is at most $6p-5$.  Since
	\[
	6p-5<p^2
	\qquad (p\geq7),
	\]
	each such $p$-divisible factor has valuation exactly one.
	
	The first crossing thresholds are
	\[
	\begin{array}{c|ccccc}
		&(\frac12)_k&(\frac16)_k&(\frac56)_k
		&(\frac43)_k&(\frac23)_k\\ \hline
		p=6m+1&3m+1&m+1&5m+1&2m&4m+1\\
		p=6m+5&3m+3&5m+5&m+1&4m+3&2m+2
	\end{array}
	\]
	
	If $p=6m+1$, then $N=3m$.  The denominator factor
	$(\frac43)_k$ first acquires a $p$-factor at $k=2m$, but
	$(\frac16)_k$ has already acquired one at $k=m+1$; moreover,
	$(\frac23)_k$ does not cross before $N$.
	
	If $p=6m+5$, then $N=3m+2$.  The denominator factor
	$(\frac23)_k$ first acquires a $p$-factor at $k=2m+2$, but
	$(\frac56)_k$ has already acquired one at $k=m+1$; moreover,
	$(\frac43)_k$ does not cross before $N$.
	
	The remaining factor $4k+1$ lies in the numerator and therefore cannot
	decrease the valuation.  Thus the denominator never contributes greater
	$p$-adic valuation than the numerator, and hence
	\[
	v_p(b_{1/6,k})\geq0.
	\]
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:C-symmetry}
	For $k\in I_p$,
	\[
	C_{N-k}\equiv C_k\pmod p.
	\]
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Put
	\[
	c_j:=
	\frac{1}{(j+\frac12)^3}
	+
	\frac{1}{(j+1)^3},
	\qquad
	C_k=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}c_j.
	\]
	Since $N\equiv-\frac12\pmod p$,
	\[
	N-\frac12-j\equiv-(j+1)\pmod p,
	\qquad
	N-j\equiv-\left(j+\frac12\right)\pmod p,
	\]
	and hence
	\[
	c_{N-1-j}\equiv-c_j\pmod p.
	\]
	It follows that $C_N\equiv0\pmod p$.  Moreover,
	\[
	C_N-C_{N-k}
	=
	\sum_{j=N-k}^{N-1}c_j
	\equiv
	-\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}c_j
	=
	-C_k
	\pmod p,
	\]
	which gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:q-antisymmetry}
	For $k\in I_p$,
	\[
	q_{N-k}\equiv-q_k\pmod p.
	\]
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
The ratio of consecutive terms is
	\[
	r_k:=
	\frac{b_{1/3,k+1}}{b_{1/3,k}}
	=
	\frac{4k+5}{4k+1}
	\frac{(k+\frac12)^4(k+\frac13)(k+\frac23)}
	{(k+1)^4(k+\frac56)(k+\frac76)}.
	\]
	As a rational function of $z$,
	\[
	r(z)\,r\left(-z-\frac32\right)=1.
	\]
	Since
	\[
	N-k-1\equiv-k-\frac32\pmod p,
	\]
	we obtain
	\[
	r_kr_{N-k-1}\equiv1\pmod p
	\]
	away from the possible central zero or pole.  Thus
	$q_{N-k}/q_k$ is constant as one moves outward through paired indices.
	
	If $N$ is odd, let $c=(N-1)/2$.  Then $N-c=c+1$ and
	$c\equiv-3/4\pmod p$, so direct substitution gives
	\[
	r_c\equiv-1\pmod p.
	\]
	If $N$ is even, let $c=N/2=(p-1)/4$.  Then $q_c=0$, and after
	cancelling the central zero and pole one obtains
	\[
	r_{c-1}r_c\equiv-1\pmod p.
	\]
	In either case the sign $-1$ propagates through all paired indices,
	which proves the result.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:initial-bridge}
	For $\rho\in\{\frac13,\frac16\}$, one has
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:initial-bridge}
		H_{p,\rho}\equiv H_\rho(-p/2)\pmod{p^3}.
	\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:cubic-collapse}
	For $\rho\in\{\frac13,\frac16\}$, one has
	\[
	J_\rho\equiv U_\rho\pmod{p^3}.
	\]
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:common-shift}
	For $\rho\in\{\frac13,\frac16\}$ and every $s\in\mathbb{Z}_p$,
	\[
	\mathcal G_\rho(s)\equiv\mathcal G_\rho(0)\pmod{p^3}.
	\]
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
The main perturbation calculation is precisely the one carried out by
	Long--Tu--Yui--Zudilin \cite[Lemma~5 and its proof]{MR4330088}.
	We record only the specialization needed here.
	
With $\alpha_\rho=\{r_1,r_2,r_3,r_4\}$ as above, set
	\[
	A_k:=\frac{\prod_{j=1}^4(r_j)_k}{(k!)^4},
	\qquad
	\gamma_\rho:=\prod_{j=1}^4\Gamma_p(r_j).
	\]
	
	For each $r_j$, let $[-r_j]_0\in\{0,1,\ldots,p-1\}$ denote the
	least nonnegative residue of $-r_j$ modulo $p$.  Then
	$r_j+[-r_j]_0$ is divisible by $p$ in $\mathbb{Z}_p$, so we may write
	\[
	r_j+[-r_j]_0=pr_j',
	\qquad r_j'\in\mathbb{Z}_p.
	\]
	
	Define
	\[
	\Lambda_{\rho,k}(s)
	:=
	\prod_{j=1}^4
	\left(1+\frac{s}{r_j'}\right)^{\nu(k,[-r_j]_0)},
	\]
	where $\nu(k,a)=0$ for $k\leq a$ and $\nu(k,a)=1$ for $k>a$.
	
	Specializing the $p$-adic perturbation expansion of
	Long--Tu--Yui--Zudilin to the datum $\alpha_\rho$ gives
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:LTYZ-specialized}
		\mathcal G_\rho(s)-\mathcal G_\rho(0)
		\equiv
		\gamma_\rho
		\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}
		A_k
		\left[
		\Lambda_{\rho,k}(s)
		\bigl(1+J_1(k)sp+J_2(k)(sp)^2\bigr)-1
		\right]
		\pmod{p^3},
	\end{equation}
	where $J_1(k)$ and $J_2(k)$ are the coefficients arising from their
	local $p$-adic gamma expansion.
	
	For $s=b\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0}$, the sum on the right-hand side of
	\eqref{eq:LTYZ-specialized} is exactly the perturbation expression
	treated in \cite[Lemma~5]{MR4330088}; hence
	\[
	\mathcal G_\rho(b)\equiv\mathcal G_\rho(0)\pmod{p^3}.
	\]
	
	It remains only to extend the parameter from
	$b\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0}$ to $s\in\mathbb{Z}_p$.
	The right-hand side of \eqref{eq:LTYZ-specialized} is a finite
	continuous $p$-adic function of $s$.  Since the nonnegative integers
	are dense in $\mathbb{Z}_p$ and $p^3\mathbb{Z}_p$ is closed, the same congruence holds
	for every $s\in\mathbb{Z}_p$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
Only the specialization $s=-\frac12$ is needed below.  Proposition
	\ref{prop:common-shift} is stated in its natural $p$-adic form because
	the same family may have other useful terminating or resonant
	specializations.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:common-final-bridge}
	For $\rho\in\left\{\frac13,\frac16\right\}$,
	one has
	\[
	R_\rho c_N^2U_\rho
	\equiv
	\left(\frac{-3}{p}\right)S_{p,\rho}
	\pmod{p^3}.
	\]
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
